name: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
role: British field marshal and Tory Prime Minister (1769-1852)
summary: Wellington, victor of Waterloo and Tory Prime Minister, defended the Established Church, the Lords and the British constitution against parliamentary reform and democracy, yet carried Catholic relief in 1829 to avert civil war.

property-fundamental.rationale: Argued against the Reform Bill that democracy would make 'property and its possessors... the common enemy' and against 'the payment of the public debt', setting its protection among the principal objects of the British Constitution.

more-religion-public.rationale: Pressed that religious instruction under the Church belong in the national system of education and in the universities, which he said must keep their tests to preserve 'any system of religion or religious instruction whatever'.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Two acts point opposite ways: in June 1828 as Prime Minister he moved the second reading of the Corn Bill, replacing prohibition by a scale of duties that kept a protective price, but in May 1846 he spoke for the Corn Importation Bill repealing the protective duties, which the Lords passed 211 to 164.

democracy-best.rationale: In the Lords on the 1831 Reform Bill he called the Commons it would produce 'a democratical assembly of the worst description', warned of 'a fierce democracy', and said 'a democracy has never been established in any part of the world, that it has not immediately declared war against property'.

separate-church-state.rationale: Opposed ending the university religious tests: if 'we have no established religion at all, every man shall follow the religion he chooses... we must make up our minds to take the consequences'.

conscription.rationale: As Chief Secretary for Ireland he brought in the 1809 Irish militia bill, giving governors power to alter the ballot lists by compulsion and letting the Lord Lieutenant substitute parish assessments or volunteering for the ballot.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: In 1839 he opposed the Order in Council on education because 'the clergy are excluded from all control', asking whether 'a tax is to be laid on them for the purpose of educating them in Popery and Unitarianism', and asked what share the Church would have in the system.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Described the King as 'the head of its political negotiations and of its armed force' in whom 'all the power is in his hands', as a feature of the constitution he defended.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Defended 'the government of King, Lords, and Commons' as it stood, warning that 'Government will become impracticable when the three branches shall be separate' and calling the system one of great advantage to the country.

non-intervention.rationale: At the Congress of Verona in 1822 he declared for the King that 'to animadvert upon the internal transactions of an independent State, unless such transactions affect the essential interests of His Majesty's subjects, is inconsistent with those principles on which His Majesty has invariably acted', refusing to join the allies' common language against Spain; a rule with a stated exception.

national-church-status.rationale: As Prime Minister he carried the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829, which opened civil and military office to Catholics but denied those so admitted any vote in appointments to benefices of the Church of England or Scotland and reserved certain offices, leaving the Established Church's status intact.

notes: A new audit built from Gurwood's collected parliamentary speeches (1854): the 1831 Reform Bill speeches, the 1829 Catholic relief and 1828 Test Act debates, the 1839 education debate and the 1809 Irish militia bill. The volumes are OCR scans, searched by theme; the slavery and Poor Law speeches in Gurwood, searched by theme, defend the West India interest and the 1834 Poor Law Commissioners but state no position on a statement. Eleven statements answered, so the uncertainty rule is not met.
